jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e106.summary: Rubric for Question 5 on the subject of theology, cross-referencing Aquinas (ST I q.1 a.7) and Capreolus, and announcing the shift to questions concerning theology's material cause or subject.

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e119.summary: States the question—whether God or something else is theology's subject—and first argument against God: every science demonstrates properties (passiones) of its subject (Posterior Analytics I), but God, having no accidents, has no properties.
claims: Every science demonstrates properties of its subject (objection)
God has no properties, so cannot be a science's subject (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e143.summary: Second argument: God cannot be subject under his absolute ratio, since an infinite thing under the ratio of infinity cannot be subject of a finite science; nor under a determinate ratio, since many things treated in theology are not attributed to God under any one special ratio.
claims: An infinite object cannot be the subject of a finite science (objection)
No single special ratio of God unifies all theology treats (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e173.summary: Third argument: a science of God would proceed either through cause or through effect, but the Trinity has no cause and cannot be concluded from effects.
claims: Theology cannot demonstrate the Trinity propter quid or quia (objection)

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e193.summary: First argument for God as subject begins: our theology has the same subject as the theology of the blessed, since they seem to differ not in object but in mode of knowing, as Paul suggests in 1 Corinthians 13.
claims: Our theology and that of the blessed differ in mode, not in object (argument)

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e206.summary: Completes the argument with 1 Cor 13 ('now through a mirror in an enigma, then face to face'): since God under his absolute ratio is the object of the blessed's knowledge, he is the subject of ours.
claims: God under his absolute ratio is the object of beatific knowledge, so also of our theology (argument)

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e219.summary: Second and third arguments for God as subject: theology is about God, creatures, or common being, but not creatures (it would treat God only as their cause) nor common being (it would not treat God and creature specifically), so it is about God; and its very name means 'discourse about God'.
claims: Theology's subject is neither creatures nor being in common, so it is God (argument)
The name 'theology' signifies discourse about God (argument)

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e243.summary: Begins the response, to be given for each of Q1's three senses of theology. First, the notion of a science's subject (the subject 'about which', not 'in which', which is the intellect) is clarified by three conditions: it is incomplex (a term); it is first and principally considered, with everything attributed to it; and things can be predicated of it denominatively. The first is argued from the subject of the demonstrated conclusion; Durandus distinguishes subject from object—the object of science being the demonstrated conclusion—so the subject/power analogy holds only regarding attribution.
claims: The subject of a science is the subject of its demonstrated conclusions, an incomplex term
The proper object of science is the demonstrated conclusion, distinct from the subject
The subject-to-science and object-to-power analogy holds only regarding attribution
concepts: subiectum de quo vs. in quo

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e332.summary: Grounds the second condition: a science's unity comes from its subject (Posterior Analytics I), which requires that the subject be principally considered and everything else be attributed to it; otherwise the science would treat diverse things as diverse.
claims: A science's unity derives from its subject
Everything treated in a science must be attributed to its subject

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e359.summary: Grounds the third condition: every science proves properties, or things in the manner of properties, of its subject, and these are predicated denominatively, so something must be predicable of the subject denominatively and not only essentially.
claims: Properties proved of a subject are predicated denominatively

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e375.summary: For theology in the first sense (assent to Scripture as taught), the subject is the meritorious or salutary act, ordinable to beatitude. First argument: the subject of a doctrine is that whose knowledge is its proximate end (in practical sciences ordered further to operation); and 2 Timothy 3 shows that Scripture's end is instruction in good work, which merits eternal life.
claims: The subject of theology in the first sense is the meritorious act
The subject of a doctrine is that whose knowledge is its proximate end
Scripture's proximate end is instruction in meritorious good works

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e432.summary: Second argument: the meritorious act is principally considered in Scripture and everything is attributed to it. All of Scripture—precepts, historical examples, wisdom counsels, prophetic rewards and punishments—clearly relates to meritorious work; even what is to be believed about God and the incarnate Son is proposed because believing is itself meritorious, because it rules and aids good work (Christ's merit restoring us to the state of meriting, his incarnation and passion as examples of humility, patience, and charity), and even the Trinity relates to merit through the difficulty of belief, its necessity for knowing the incarnate person, and its promised clear understanding as reward.
claims: Everything in Scripture is attributed to meritorious work
Believing the articles is itself a meritorious act
Christ's incarnation and passion restore us to meriting and serve as examples
The article of the Trinity is ordered to merit by the difficulty of belief and the promised reward of understanding

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e573.summary: Confirms with scriptural authorities calling Scripture the 'science of salvation' (Prov 8, Luke 1, Rom 1, Acts 13) and Augustine (faith, hope, charity as the aim of all divine works; whoever keeps charity holds all of Scripture). The necessity of Scripture lies precisely in ordering humans to supernatural beatitude through meritorious works, so meritorious work is its principal concern; those who deny this have not read Scripture or turn away from it.
claims: Scripture is the science of salvation
The necessity of revealed Scripture lies in directing human acts to supernatural beatitude
Meritorious work is the principal concern of Scripture

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e643.summary: Answers the objection that, since first-sense theology equals faith and faith's articles are about God, its subject cannot be meritorious work. Faith taken in its full breadth equals this theology and has the same subject; faith narrowly as 'faith of the articles' concerns God, but under the ratio of Saviour, and even so its articles are attributed to salutary work, as the Nicene Creed's 'for us and for our salvation' shows. Like a sailor who considers the stars only as rules for navigation, faith and Scripture consider the incarnate, suffering God as aids for sailing to the port of salvation; so meritorious work, not God, is the subject.
claims: Faith in its full breadth has meritorious work as its subject
Faith of the articles concerns God under the ratio of Saviour
Scripture considers God not absolutely but as directing us to salvation, as navigation considers stars

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e747.summary: For theology in the second (defensive) sense, the subject is God. The subject of a science is the subject of its principally inferred conclusion, and defensive theology principally defends and declares the articles about God in himself or incarnate. Other scriptural truths (e.g. that love of God merits eternal life, from John 14) follow easily once the articles are granted, so Scripture needs defense only regarding its principles—the articles about God.
claims: The subject of defensive theology is God
Defensive theology principally defends and declares the articles about God
Scripture needs defense only regarding its principles, the articles, not its easily derived conclusions

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e829.summary: Asks under what ratio God is subject, and presents the opinion that it is the absolute ratio. First proof: the formal ratio of the subject must contain everything treated in the science (as the physician considers the nerve only as receptive of health), but no attributive ratio (such as glorifier) can contain substantial predicates or what belongs to God absolutely, like being eternal and triune.
claims: The formal ratio of the subject must encompass everything treated in the science (opinion)
No attributive or relational ratio of God can encompass what is said of God absolutely (opinion)

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e886.summary: Second proof of that opinion: what a science seeks to prove of something is a property, not the subject's formal ratio; theology asks whether God is glorifier as it asks whether he is wise or omnipotent, so 'glorifier' cannot be the subject's formal ratio.
claims: What a science proves of its subject cannot be the subject's formal ratio (opinion)

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e912.summary: Durandus's position: God is subject of defensive theology under a determinate ratio. God is subject under the same ratio in this theology and in faith of the articles, since the articles are its principal conclusions—theology and faith differ only in mode of assent. But in faith of the articles God cannot be subject under the absolute ratio, because under that ratio many things are demonstrable (that God is one, intellectual), whereas no article is demonstrable to a wayfarer.
claims: God is subject of defensive theology under a determinate, not the absolute, ratio
Defensive theology and faith of the articles share the same subject, differing only in mode of assent
Since many truths about God absolutely are demonstrable and no article is, the articles do not concern God under his absolute ratio

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e982.summary: Identifies the ratio as that of Saviour: it is principally intended in faith—there was never faith, before or after the Fall, without explicit faith in the Saviour—and it implicitly contains the other articles (incarnation, passion, resurrection, ascension, judgment) which explain how God worked our salvation, and even the Trinity, through the determination of the saving person.
claims: God is subject of faith of the articles under the ratio of Saviour
Faith has always been explicitly faith in the Saviour
The ratio of Saviour implicitly contains all other articles, including the Trinity

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1019.summary: Second argument for the ratio of Saviour: God is subject under the ratio most related to meritorious work, since the articles are principles for Scripture's conclusions about meritorious work; the ratio of Saviour includes salvation as end and implicitly the way to it, and in practical matters the end functions as principle. The name 'Saviour' given to the one all the articles speak of (Matthew 1, Luke 1–2) confirms this.
claims: The articles are principles for conclusions about meritorious work
The ratio of Saviour includes the end of meritorious work and the means to it
God under the ratio of Saviour is the subject of faith of the articles and defensive theology
concepts: end as principle in practical matters

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1069.summary: Replies to the first proof of the absolute-ratio opinion: granted that the subject contains all things, attribution to the formal ratio is in the order of cognition, not of being (in physics, quantity and matter–form composition are attributed to mobility though they cause it), so absolute and substantial predicates can be attributed to a relational ratio like Saviour, as God's operations ad extra lead to knowledge of his absolute perfections. Moreover, demonstrable predicates about God (e.g. intellectual substance) do not properly belong to theology, as Augustine indicates; they are presupposed from metaphysics or natural science, and the theologian who inquires into them takes the philosopher's role.
claims: Attribution to the subject's formal ratio follows the order of knowing, not of being
Absolute predicates of God can be attributed to the relational ratio of Saviour
Demonstrable truths about God belong to metaphysics, not properly to theology
concepts: order of cognition vs. order of being

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1172.summary: Reply to the second proof: theology presupposes that God is Saviour and inquires into how (through incarnation, passion, etc.); asking whether God is Saviour is like the natural philosopher asking whether anything is mobile.
claims: Theology presupposes that God is Saviour and inquires how he saves

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1192.summary: For theology in the third (deductive) sense: Durandus doubts anything properly speculative is deduced from the articles, but if so its subject is the same as that of faith of the articles, since the article serves as minor premise whose subject becomes the conclusion's subject (e.g. 'where there is unity of essence in several supposits, distinction is not by absolutes; God is so; therefore...'). Speculative deduction perfects the intellect little, but practical deductions (humility from Christ's self-emptying, Phil 2; endurance from his passion, 1 Pet 2) greatly move affection and good work; since Scripture itself makes these deductions, deductive theology coincides with Scripture and its subject is meritorious work.
claims: If anything speculative were deduced from the articles, its subject would be that of the articles
Speculative deduction from the articles perfects the intellect little
Practical deductions from the articles move affection and good works
Deductive theology coincides with Scripture and has meritorious work as its subject
concepts: minor premise and subject of conclusion

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1292.summary: Reply to the first initial argument: Aristotle's dictum concerns propter quid science, demonstrating a property of the subject through its cause; quia science, from effect to cause, may conclude only that the cause exists or is intelligent, willing, etc., which need differ from the subject only in reason. Thus both acquired and infused science of God is possible.
claims: Quia science need not demonstrate really distinct properties of its subject
Properties of God need differ from him only in reason

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1323.summary: Reply to the second initial argument: God is subject of defensive theology under the ratio of Saviour, to which all is attributed. But the infinity argument against the absolute ratio fails: a finite science can treat the infinite, whether as the privation of limit (the same science considers habit and privation, as Aristotle treats the infinite in Physics III) or as the thing subject to infinity; the blessed's finite knowledge has God absolutely as object; and science takes its character from its object, but not univocally—a science of motion is not mobile.
claims: God is subject of defensive theology under the ratio of Saviour
A finite science can have the infinite as object
Science derives its ratio from its object but not univocally

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1393.summary: Reply to the third initial argument: strict science of the Trinity is impossible, by cause or effect, but broadly taken—any declarative knowledge of the articles by authority or probable appearances that can persuade—such science exists, and this is theology.
claims: Strict science of the Trinity is impossible for us
Theology is science only broadly, as declarative and persuasive knowledge of the articles

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1413.summary: Reply to the first contrary argument: the wayfarer's declarative knowledge and the beatific science differ not only in light and mode but in object: beatific knowledge, our reward, has God under the ratio able to fill the intellect's capacity, while knowledge in via directs to merit and so concerns God as Saviour. Because the absolute ratio is wider and includes the ratio of Saviour, heavenly vision clarifies all that faith now sees enigmatically, surpassing rather than merely matching it.
claims: Wayfarer's theology and beatific knowledge differ in object as well as mode
Beatific knowledge concerns God under the ratio that fills the intellect; wayfarer's theology concerns God as Saviour
Vision will succeed faith regarding the same things, but exceed it

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1451.summary: Reply to the second contrary argument: theology, however taken, considers God not according to what belongs to him absolutely but only in relation to creatures; so the ratio of Saviour is relational.
claims: Theology considers God only in relation to creatures

jsnvu6-d1e133-d1e1464.summary: Reply to the third contrary argument: a habit is not always named from the formal ratio of its subject but sometimes from what is more dignified; since in the work of our salvation God's part is more dignified than ours, the science of our salvation is named theology after God.
claims: A habit may be named from what is more dignified rather than from its subject
Theology is named from God because God's part in salvation is the more dignified

jsnvu6-d1e133.summary: Question 5 asks what the subject of theology is—God or something else. After defining the subject of a science by three conditions (incomplex, principally considered with all else attributed to it, bearing denominative predicates) and distinguishing it from the object (the demonstrated conclusion), Durandus answers according to Q1's three senses. For theology as assent to Scripture (equivalent to faith in its full breadth), the subject is the meritorious act ordered to beatitude: Scripture's end is instruction in good works, everything in it—precepts, examples, counsels, rewards, and even the articles—is attributed to meritorious work, as a sailor considers the stars only for navigation. For defensive theology, whose principal conclusions are the articles, the subject is God—not under his absolute ratio, under which much is demonstrable, but under the ratio of Saviour, which faith always explicitly concerned, which implicitly contains all the articles, and which most directly relates to merit; demonstrable truths about God belong to metaphysics. For deductive theology, speculative deductions are negligible, practical ones coincide with Scripture, so the subject is again meritorious work. Replies defend quia science of God, the possibility of finite knowledge of the infinite, theology as science only broadly, and the difference in object between wayfarer and blessed.
claims: The subject of a science is incomplex, principally considered, and admits denominative predication
The subject of theology as assent to Scripture is the meritorious act ordered to beatitude
The subject of defensive theology is God under the ratio of Saviour, not under his absolute ratio
Demonstrable truths about God properly belong to metaphysics rather than theology
Deductive theology coincides with Scripture and has meritorious work as its subject
Theology in via and beatific knowledge differ in object as well as in mode
